newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nippon Life, Sanyo agree on loan repayment delay.
newsitem.headline: Nippon Life, Sanyo agree on loan repayment delay.

text.p: Nippon Life Insurance Co, a top Japanese life insurer, on Thursday said it agreed with Sanyo Securities Co Ltd to delay the repayment of the brokerage's subordinated loans from the insurer by three months.

In exchange for accepting Sanyo's request to delay repayment of the loans, which were due at the end of July 1998, a spokesman for Nippon Life said Sanyo had agreed to draft a new restructuring plan within the three-month period.
A Sanyo spokesman said he could not immediately confirm the agreement. The second-tier brokerage has a total of 20 billion yen worth of subordinated loans from nine Japanese life insurers.
Of that, Nippon Life has the largest share with four billion yen in loans to Sanyo, which are repayable only after debts with higher priority have been honoured.

A spokesman for Dai-Ichi Mutual Life Insurance Co, which has subordinated loans of three billion yen to Sanyo, told Reuters that the companies had not reached an agreement yet on any delays in the loan repayments.
It was not immediately clear whether other life insurers would agree to a delay, but industry sources said they were likely to move in the same direction as Nippon Life.

News of the agreement boosted Sanyo shares, which earlier fell to an all-time low of 138 yen on the Tokyo bourse. As of 0539 GMT, the shares had recovered sharply to 163 yen, up 19 yen from Wednesday's close, making the firm the top percentage gainer on the first section of the Tokyo bourse.
Lingering financial jitters over Sanyo, burdened with bad assets at its financial and real-estate affiliates, have been behind the weakness in its shares.

If there had been no agreement on the delay by the end of Thursday, Sanyo's capital adequacy ratio could have fallen below 120 percent, a level at which the Finance Ministry would have ordered the brokerage to take more drastic restructuring measures to improve its operations, industry sources said.
Subordinated loans cease to be regarded as part of an institution's capital once the remaining period to maturity falls below one year. At that point, the loans are treated as short-term debt.
In 1994, Sanyo embarked on a nine-year restructuring plan to help bail out its non-bank financial affiliates with the support of three major creditor banks and Nomura Securities Co Ltd.

But the latest agreement could be only a stop-gap measure, industry sources said, as it was not immediately clear whether the troubled brokerage would be able to come up with a more drastic restructuring plan during the next three months.
